name: Neville Chamberlain
role: British prime minister (1937–1940), Chancellor of the Exchequer (1931–1937)
summary: A Conservative who as Minister of Health and Chancellor favoured tariffs, balanced budgets and private enterprise, and as prime minister pursued appeasement of Germany and Italy until the March 1939 seizure of Prague, then rearmed, introduced compulsory military training and took Britain to war over Poland.

booksNotUsed.reason: How We Are Fed is a school geography reader by another author with the same surname (James Franklin Chamberlain), not by Neville Chamberlain.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He held that the State rarely shows it can run an industry better than private enterprise, though he accepted tariffs and state aid to areas in distress.

public-ownership.rationale: He said the circumstances would have to be very exceptional for the State to show it could conduct an industry better than private enterprise.

free-trade.rationale: As Chancellor he enacted a general tariff on imports in place of free trade; the same debate records him using it to bargain other countries' duties down.

land-value-tax.rationale: As Chancellor he confirmed in 1932 that the Land Value Tax was to be suspended, and no land tax replaced other taxes under him.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: As Chancellor he carried the Import Duties Act 1932 and defended it as moving work from foreign factories and fields to British ones and protecting the home market.

conscription.rationale: His government introduced compulsory military training in 1939 and he moved the bill himself, reversing an earlier pledge against peacetime conscription.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His 1936 Budget raised taxes so that defence spending was paid for rather than borrowed, and he balanced the Budgets of 1932-36; the 1937 defence loans were for rearmament, not stimulus.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: He defended the 1927 Act's limits on sympathetic strikes and said it was better to prevent such strikes than to wait and control them.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: In 1939 his government entered a treaty of mutual responsibilities with Turkey, which he reported to the House; earlier he had avoided firm commitments.

collective-defense.rationale: His government signed the 1939 treaty with Turkey, which he reported to the House as a defensive instrument creating mutual responsibilities to oppose aggression.

notes: Searched the Commons Hansard corpus (his speeches 1919-1940) and historic-hansard pages by theme: tariffs and trade, strikes and unions, taxation and the capital levy, land and housing, Poor Law and pensions, nationalisation and private enterprise, budgets and deficits, conscription and defence, alliances and guarantees, the League and sanctions, Munich and self-determination, Ireland, India, Palestine, refugees, emergency powers. Most of these turned up government business or answers to questions rather than a position on a statement, so the rest stay null. His mature position on conscription changed in 1939 from an earlier pledge against it.
